data.title: Inner London house prices post largest annual drop since 2009 amid soaring mortgage costs
data.description:
HOUSE prices in inner London fell the most since the financial crisis, according to official statistics that highlight the impact of soaring mortgage costs on the capital. 

Average values in the boroughs declined 7.2 per cent to £621,491 (US$818,570) in the 12 months through September, the largest annual drop since August 2009, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Wednesday (Nov 18), citing Land Registry data.

Across the capital, prices posted a smaller decline of 3.5 per cent.

Home values in the central parts of London have fallen in all but three of the past 12 months.

Prices in Westminster and Kensington & Chelsea – two of London’s most exclusive areas –  are down 18.5 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, since September 2025.

The Iran energy crisis has pushed up borrowing costs, stretching affordability for prospective buyers.

Key mortgage rates have climbed close to 6 per cent, up from 4.83 per cent just before the start of the conflict.

Aspiring homeowners in expensive areas like London, where house prices are still about twice the UK average, are disproportionately affected because they have to come up with larger deposits and take on more debt.

“House price-to-income ratios are more stretched in inner London, which makes prices much more susceptible to rises in interest rates, and we’ve had three big leg ups in mortgage costs lately” said Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills in London. 

He added that the prime sector has also been hit by the government taxes on the most expensive properties, as well as volatile geopolitics. 

The downturn has wiped £23,000 off the value of an average home in London since their peak in July 2025, the ONS figures show.

Flats, which have underperformed other types of property, account for around half of all sales in London compared with a fifth in Britain as a whole.

The Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in over three years in November, and officials signalled they could deliver another hike as soon as December to fight off inflationary pressures.

Across the UK, house prices rose 1.2 per cent in the year to September, a rate that was unchanged from the previous month. While values declined in London and the South East, regions like the North East and the North West recorded strong increases. 

The report adds to mounting evidence of broader pressure on the housing market.

Demand for home loans has hit its lowest in 33 months, and property surveyors warned home values could drop 1 per cent in the year ahead as the sales outlook deteriorates. Lender Nationwide also said house prices stagnated in October due to high mortgage costs. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Prioritise resilience over innovation in building digital payment rails, say central bank panellists
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Central banks need to prioritise resilience when issuing digital money and developing payment rails, as it is the foundation for consumer protection and inclusion, said panellists at the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF).

While continued innovation is important, it should proceed with safeguards and collaboration between regulators and the industry, given that it is central banks’ job to maintain trust in the financial system, they said on Friday (Nov 20).

“In the end, the best system – in my opinion – will not be the one who uses the new technology the fastest, but the one that keeps improving while keeping people’s trust in the financial system,” said Ahmed bin Khalid Al-Thani, deputy governor of the Qatar Central Bank.

Ahmed was speaking at a panel discussion about what it will take to build a trusted multi-rail financial system at SFF.

With him were Chea Serey, governor of the National Bank of Cambodia; Piero Cipollone, a member of the executive board at the European Central Bank; Swaminathan Janakiraman, deputy governor of the Reserve Bank of India; and Leong Sing Chiong, deputy managing director (markets and development) at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

The session was moderated by Maha El Dimachki, managing director for policy and skilling at the Global Finance & Technology Network.

Discussing trade-offs between innovation, resilience, consumer protection and inclusion, Ahmed said resilience is not separated from inclusion or customer protection.

Any systemic disruptions will disproportionately affect those with fewer financial options, he noted.

This is especially when digital payment systems have reached a scale that makes it public infrastructure.

Citing India’s Unified Payments Interface as an example, which handled an average 800 million plus transactions every day, Janakiraman noted a few outages could be a loss of one day’s business or income for a vegetable vendor or a tea stall owner.

“That brings us, as a regulator, enormous responsibility to ensure that the system’s resilience and integrity are preserved at all times,” he said.

Cipollone also expects central banks to make sure that inclusiveness is essential in financial systems.

“As a central bank, you should not gather only for people that love innovation for the sake of innovation, or early adopters that are willing to take some risk in order to experiment,” he said.

“We are together for the needs of (the whole) population, and (should) not forget the marginal ones.”

But MAS’ Leong noted the need to balance between innovation, allowing for innovation versus preserving safety and soundness.

Hence, Leong said the opportunity in Singapore is for MAS to collaborate with the industry to figure out how best to strike that balance, both in terms of growth opportunities as well as safety and soundness.

This is especially so as central banks and financial institutions alike have similar concerns, which is to maintain trust and reputation while being able to continuously innovate.

“It is not so much the central bank versus tech companies versus financial institutions,” Leong said. “Everybody has a common interest, recognising that the foundation of finance is trust.”

data.title: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
data.description:
[TAIPEI] Taiwan’s TSMC is tightening restrictions on Chinese chip designers, suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders and generally limiting affected customers to older chipmaking technology, said two people familiar with the matter.

The move could close one of the last remaining routes for Chinese companies to produce powerful artificial intelligence processors, complicating Beijing’s efforts to develop domestic alternatives to chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by TSMC.

The world’s largest contract chipmaker has instructed that affected orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below be halted, unless customers obtain US export licences, the people said.

Chinese designers will generally be limited to older 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided their chips do not use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) or require advanced packaging, going by the TSMC guidance reviewed by the two people.

Most leading AI chips are produced using 7-nanometre processes or smaller, enabling faster and more energy-efficient performance.

HBM allows processors to handle the vast data volumes required by AI applications, while advanced packaging integrates chips and memory to boost computing power.

US closes manufacturing route

The restrictions follow new US Commerce Department rules that took effect on Thursday (Nov 19), removing a compliance route that had allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced manufacturing services without individual export licences.

“TSMC is aware of and will comply with the new Bureau of Industry and Security regulations as applicable,” the company said in an e-mail to Reuters on Friday, adding it does not comment on market rumours.

Previously, it could check the computing power and other technical characteristics of certain Chinese chip designs to determine whether they fell outside US export controls.

Under the new rules, it can no longer use that verification process for affected Chinese customers. Their advanced chips are instead presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless an exception applies.

The Financial Times first reported on Thursday that TSMC and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following the new restrictions.

China’s AI chip ambitions

The measures could particularly affect Chinese companies developing alternatives to Nvidia’s processors, including independent chip designers and tech giants that have developed in-house chips.

A US government list of approved chip designers includes Nvidia, AMD, Apple and Taiwanese companies MediaTek and Realtek, but no mainland Chinese firms.

Some Chinese AI chip designers still had access to TSMC’s 7-nanometre manufacturing technology before Thursday, a separate source with direct knowledge of the matter said.

Reuters could not independently verify the arrangements under which those chips were manufactured.

TSMC’s guidance also requires closer scrutiny of customers’ operating locations, parent companies, major shareholders, packaging providers and shipping routes, the two people familiar with the matter said.

The checks extend to orders placed through overseas subsidiaries or intermediaries, including entities in Taiwan, the US, Europe, Japan and South-east Asia. REUTERS

data.title: Singapore-based DayOne is said to pause US IPO plans on data centre, market concerns
data.description:
[HONG KONG] DayOne Data Centres has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, people familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.

The data centre operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously.

But it started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.

Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.

The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.

Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the people said. A representative for DayOne declined to comment.

Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.

The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6 per cent in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.

Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement and rose 17 per cent on its trading debut on Thursday, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.

Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever IPOs, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data centre development, fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba.

The US this week put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators they’ll need a license to purchase American tech hardware.

DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Working on my own terms
data.description:
AT 76, I still look forward to having something meaningful to do each day.

My golden years give me greater freedom to choose how I spend my time, be it by contributing through work, sharing what I have learnt, serving the community or enjoying the people and pursuits that enrich my life.

Recently, my Raffles Institution cohort celebrated the 60 years since completing our O levels in 1966. Many schoolmates have retired and are enjoying travel, family life and community service.

I am among the few who continue to work. Our paths differ, but we all face a worthwhile question: How do we make these years fulfilling?

A fulfilling life need not include paid work, a board appointment or a crowded diary. It can be found in caring for family, pursuing a new hobby, joining a community group or being a dependable mentor.

What matters is that the individual remains interested in life and connected to others.

Work with a different purpose

At this stage, work is less about earning money and more about engaging my mind and putting my experience to good use.

Board discussions and advisory assignments require me to listen carefully, question assumptions and consider unfamiliar problems. They are a form of mental gymnastics I enjoy, and I hope such stimulating intellectual challenges will keep dementia at bay.

My corporate roles also connect me with people across countries, industries and generations. Experience gives me a perspective to offer, though I do not assume to have all the answers. Younger colleagues often help me see fresh possibilities.

Having spent more than 30 years as a CEO, technopreneur and private investor, including my tenure as vice-president and managing director for the Asia-Pacific at Compaq, I have helped businesses with listings, mergers, accelerated growth and turnarounds.

These experiences have value beyond the positions I once held. The lessons learnt from difficult decisions, mistakes and setbacks can help others navigate their own challenges. Our usefulness does not end when our formal careers do.

Share what experience has taught us

Teaching entrepreneurship and leadership at the National University of Singapore, alongside mentoring members of the Singapore Institute of Directors and other professional networks, have allowed me to pass on some of these lessons. Knowledge accumulated over five decades should be passed on.

Mentoring is a rewarding way for seniors to contribute, and it need not happen through a formal programme. We can help a young colleague think through a career decision or encourage someone recovering from a setback. Sometimes, attentive listening is more useful than advice.

Learning also flows both ways. Younger people bring fresh perspectives and introduce unfamiliar technologies. Seniors should remain willing to learn and ask for help.

Find fulfilment in service

Public and community service have brought me deep fulfilment.

Through my mediation work with the State Courts and community centres, I have helped people resolve disputes in business and with family and neighbours.

When parties reach a settlement, I feel privileged to have helped them find a way forward – a reminder to be grateful for the peace in my own life.

I also served as a Justice of the Peace for 15 years and continue to solemnise marriages. Helping couples begin their journey together is a joy; it gives me an opportunity to share advice drawn from my former leadership roles at the National Family Council and the Centre for Fathering.

Service is open to all of us. A senior need not chair an organisation to make a difference. Reading with a child, visiting someone who lives alone or calling a withdrawn friend can be a meaningful contribution. We can all give the gift of time.

Discover new interests

Writing has enabled me to turn reflections into something useful to others. I have authored six books – including Golden Nuggets, an anthology of stories by seniors – which have collectively raised more than S$3 million for charities.

But we do not need to publish a book to preserve our stories; recording these tales or sharing memories with grandchildren leaves a precious inheritance.

Another source of pleasure is birding, which I took up five years ago after a slipped disc led me to give up golf. It has brought me to local spots like Kranji Marshes and overseas locations in search of unfamiliar species.

My camera now accompanies me on business trips to cities from London to Shanghai, and I go birding whenever time permits.

Birding has taught me to slow down and enjoy discovery. For other seniors, that delight may come from painting, cooking or learning about artificial intelligence.

We are never obliged to remain the people our careers required us to be.

Plan for the next chapter

Staying active requires judgment. Health, mobility and finances differ. During illness or recovery, participation may take a quieter form: a telephone conversation, reading or light activity with a friend.

Accepting help can make continued engagement possible.

We must also be willing to let go of roles that no longer fit. Saying “yes” to purpose sometimes requires saying “no” to more activity, ensuring we make time for relationships that are central to the lives we enjoy. Making time for my wife, children, children-in-law and grandchildren is as worthwhile as any professional achievement.

Earlier as an engineering student, I developed a life plan with three stages.

In Plan A, I would work for others and for money. In my current Plan B, I let others and money work for me, giving me greater freedom to choose my contributions.

In Plan C, which I intend to move towards at 80, I hope to devote more time to two areas spelled with a capital “C” – Church and Charity – and less to the smaller “c” – corporate commitments – while retaining selected engagements where I can be useful.

Crucially, the plan can evolve. Its value is that it encourages me to think deliberately about how I want to live.

The average lifespan of a Singaporean man is 84 years. Theoretically, I have eight more years to live, but that is not a given. I prefer to treat that uncertainty as a reason to appreciate today.

For seniors wondering where to begin, choose one manageable step: contact a friend, explore a hobby, learn something unfamiliar or offer an hour of help. Each is a reason to look forward to tomorrow.

I share my journey to encourage active, joyful ageing. There is still much to enjoy, discover and contribute. “No time” should never be an excuse to pursue a worthwhile purpose.

If I can have a vertical take-off from the short runway ahead of me, I will seize it to enjoy my life to the fullest.

For these reasons, retirement is not in my vocabulary.

The writer is the former vice-president and managing director of Compaq Computer Asia-Pacific. He is also a board member, senior advisor, adjunct professor and mediator.

Switching Lanes is a column exploring the diverse realities of life after a full-time career. From finding fresh purpose to savouring newfound freedom, we are redefining retirement.

Have a perspective to share? Write to btletter@sph.com.sg with the subject, Switching Lanes.

data.title: The US housing marketâs widening wealth gap comes down to luck and timing
data.description:
[BOSTON] In today’s US housing market, whether you are a winner or a loser comes down to a quirk of timing.

Roughly 2.4 million homeowners with mortgages are sitting on at least US$1 million in equity, almost triple the number before the pandemic-era boom and near a record.

At the other extreme, more than 1.1 million borrowers owe more than their homes are worth, according to data from Intercontinental Exchange as at September.

The two groups are a stark illustration of a housing market that has become increasingly frozen and divided.

Pending home sales plunged in October to a record low, the National Association of Realtors reported on Wednesday (Nov 18), as elevated borrowing costs discourage buyers.

The average 30-year mortgage rate climbed to 7.28 per cent this week, the ninth straight week above 7 per cent.

With the US Federal Reserve widely expected to raise interest rates in December, there is little prospect of relief anytime soon. 

How homeowners are faring depends largely on when they got in.

Millions who bought when rates were historically low are sitting on enormous gains with cheap loans that they are reluctant to give up.

Those who entered later face an opposite reality: higher borrowing costs and homes purchased near peak prices.

“Equity largely boils down to timing and location,” said Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at Intercontinental Exchange.

“People who bought before 2022 have ridden years of price growth. Those who bought more recently, especially in the South and West with a low down payment, have a lot less cushion.”

The consequences have the potential to extend well beyond the current housing cycle. Families with substantial home equity have an asset they can draw on to help the next generation buy houses, pay for education or meet other major expenses, potentially extending their advantage for decades.

Even without selling, equity-rich homeowners can borrow against their properties to help adult children with down payments or co-sign mortgages, said Dowell Myers, an urban planner and demographer at the University of Southern California.

For families with little or no equity, that type of financial support is largely unavailable. 

“There’s a class divide,” Myers said. “The American Dream is that everybody has a chance to break through, and that’s more and more difficult as houses get more expensive and the entry cost gets higher and higher.”

South, West troubles

Much of the home equity divide also comes down to geography. While the number of equity millionaires rose 6 per cent nationally in September from a year earlier, it jumped 31 per cent in Chicago, 22 per cent in New York, 19 per cent in Philadelphia and 16 per cent in Houston, according to Intercontinental Exchange data.

At the other end of the spectrum are parts of the South and West, where prices have retreated from their peaks, the firm’s data show.

In Cape Coral, Florida, 11.2 per cent of mortgaged homeowners are underwater, followed by Lakeland, Florida, at 8.9 per cent and Austin, at 8.4 per cent.

Dallas has the greatest number of underwater borrowers of any major market, about 63,000.

Even within the same region, the fortunes of homeowners can be dramatically different.

In the Kingston area of New York’s picturesque Hudson Valley, real estate agent Kate Quintard has clients preparing to cash in on the pandemic housing boom.

The empty-nester couple from New Jersey bought a 3,800-square-foot house with sweeping views of the Catskills for US$445,000 in 2019, then added a heated pool and outdoor entertainment space. Their adult children spent part of the pandemic there.

As the children started families of their own, the couple found themselves using the property less often. They listed it for US$1.425 million in October, and it is now under contract for more than US$1 million above what they originally paid.

“They are over the moon,” Quintard said. “They didn’t expect it to go like that.”

Craig Smith, who works alongside Quintard on Compass’ Upstate Curious team, had a buyer who lost out in the recent bidding war for that property.

But the market has cooled considerably, he said, and other sellers have had a much tougher time.

One of them bought a house in the city of Hudson for US$425,000 in 2019 then spent about US$400,000 adding an accessory dwelling unit and a climate-controlled one-car garage.

After two price cuts, the property is listed for US$799,000, less than the combined cost of the purchase and improvements. Six similarly priced homes are for sale on the same street.

“Buyers are sitting on the sidelines until it’s turnkey and special, and then they’re fighting for the same house,” Smith said. “A group of sellers waited too long, and the market slowed down.”

For many homeowners, there has been little reason to test the market and give up low-rate mortgages. Their decision to stay put has limited the supply of homes for sale, helping sustain property values and preserve wealth accumulated during the boom.

But prices are beginning to weaken in places where more homes are coming onto the market.

In areas such as Austin and Denver, higher borrowing costs have discouraged house hunters even as inventory has grown, putting downward pressure on prices.

Recent buyers who had low down payments are particularly exposed.

Some 88 per cent of underwater mortgages were taken out in 2022 or later, according to Intercontinental Exchange.

Their numbers have climbed almost 30 per cent over the past year to the highest level for this time of year since 2017, though at about 2 per cent of mortgage holders, the share remains very low by the standards of the post-2008 financial crisis.

But even housing winners are subject to quirks of timing. Home equity gains depend on values holding up, and someone being willing to pay for the house.

“It’s all paper wealth until they start selling,” Myers said. “It all depends on them having a future buyer.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: No free lunch: South-east Asiaâs price controls become harder to sustain
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] At supermarket counters from Kuala Lumpur to Manila, global macroeconomic shocks have been jacking up grocery bills – while extracting much higher costs from many governments.

In much of South-east Asia, food carries a significant weight in the consumer price index basket. The prolonged shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up global oil prices, in turn raising transportation, logistics and production costs. Higher fertiliser prices have also made agricultural production costlier, while El Nino-related weather conditions have hit crop yields.

But these cost increases have not uniformly translated to higher consumer prices at the till – partly because some governments have stepped in to cap prices or offer subsidies.

Can they afford to keep intervening to protect household purchasing power?

Established caps

“Countries with larger buffers, stronger currencies or diversified import sources can absorb more of the shock,” says Maybank analyst Brian Lee. “Countries with thin inventories or greater import dependence are considerably more exposed.”

Food prices in the Philippines rose by 6.4 per cent year on year in October, down slightly from inflation of 6.8 per cent in September. Yet rice prices in the country – which produces more than 70 per cent of its rice supply domestically – still picked up at a faster clip.

Food has been a key driver of headline inflation in the Philippines. Catharine Kho, a senior economist at the Asean+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (Amro), notes that heavy rains and flooding disrupted production and deliveries recently, while “higher fuel costs and a weaker peso added to these pressures”.

That’s even though countries such as the Philippines and Indonesia have stockpiles of staples such as rice to serve as what Amro economist Ravisara Hataiseree calls “strategic food reserves… to buffer against sudden supply disruptions”.

At the same time, another factor determining the extent of cost pass-through in developing economies has been state controls on the prices of staples.

Price controls are well established in the region, where policymakers favour mandatory price ceilings for providing immediate and highly visible relief to keep essential goods affordable, while subsidies are preferred for preserving the incentive to produce or supply goods.

As Lee points out: “For staples such as rice, sugar and cooking oil, governments are more inclined to intervene because consumption is widespread, these goods carry high social and political salience, and poorer households spend a larger share of their income on them.”

RHB group chief economist Barnabas Gan comments that food inflation in Malaysia has “remained relatively contained compared to what would otherwise have been expected”, thanks in part to its price controls on a range of grocery staples.

Notably, Malaysia has capped the price of standard coarse white sugar at RM2.85 (US$0.70) per kilogram since 2018. This is among the lowest prices in the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economists Ahmad Mobeen, Lei Yi and Harumi Taguchi, who highlight Malaysia’s “longstanding system of administered prices”.

While direct consumer subsidies for sugar were abolished in 2013, Malaysia has offered incentives to sugar refiners since late 2023, to maintain retail price stability.

Responsive rollouts

Beyond long-running schemes, governments may also step in on an ad-hoc basis to manage prices – such as the Philippines’ imposition, in May, of a 50-peso (US$0.79) ceiling on certain rice imports for 30 days.

In response to the weather-related production declines, the Indonesian government in early November announced that it would distribute one million tonnes of rice through its existing Food Supply and Price Stabilisation programme at 12,500 rupiah (US$0.68) per kilogram, below the market rate of between 15,000 and 17,000 rupiah per kilogram.

Established schemes to tackle fuel costs – another common target of government price controls – have taken on increased prominence in the wake of the global energy shock too.

For instance, Thailand has an oil fuel fund that the government taps to compensate for the increase in retail fuel prices when oil prices surge.

Nomura chief Asean economist Euben Paracuelles sees a sharp divergence in energy price increases across South-east Asian states depending on whether they maintain fuel subsidies.

Malaysia uses subsidies to maintain RON95 fuel prices at RM1.99 per litre for eligible residents, while Indonesia keeps subsidised prices for RON90 petrol at 10,000 rupiah per litre and for biodiesel blend at 6,800 rupiah per litre.

Such fuel subsidies have been effective in curbing inflation, with levels within authorities’ target ranges, Paracuelles says.

He pointed out that Malaysia and Indonesia have seen zero increase in subsidised retail fuel prices since the global energy crisis began with the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East in February. 

At the opposite extreme, the Philippines has no measures to tackle fuel price changes – “so the pass-through is quick and very large”, he said, with 50 to 60 per cent jumps in retail fuel prices in the same period.

Such moves come as more than 80 per cent of Asia-Pacific economies have introduced measures to dampen the pass-through of higher energy prices since February, according to an October regional assessment by the International Monetary Fund.

Conversely, Singapore manages inflation through an exchange rate-based monetary policy and direct household support in the form of vouchers, rebates and payouts. The government explicitly avoids enforcing price ceilings or subsidies to prevent market distortions.

But the National Trades Union Congress-affiliated FairPrice Group (FPG) implements voluntary, time-limited price freezes and discounts on daily essentials. In October, it lowered prices for chicken and eggs – two popular protein staples – until the end of 2026.

In all, FPG has committed more than S$7.5 million worth of savings on groceries and household essentials in 2026, which the retailer attributed in part to concerns over global uncertainty and potential pressure on food and commodity prices.

FPG may be able to negotiate with suppliers for lower prices or absorb some of the higher costs by accepting lower margins, according to Chua Yeow Hwee, an assistant professor of economics at Nanyang Technological University.

S&P’s team adds that the market leader’s pricing decisions may also exert some competitive pressure on other retailers and keep a lid on price increases in the market.

Still, watchers say the overall impact of such voluntary price controls on inflation is likely limited. 

As a profit-seeking entity, FPG is limited by its own financial resources, despite its social mandate, UOB head of research Suan Teck Kin observes.

The S&P analysts add that such initiatives “cannot fully offset sustained increases in global food, energy, fertiliser or freight costs, particularly given Singapore’s high dependence on imported food”.

Price controls’ high costs

Government price controls may be effective in keeping price rises at bay – to some extent.

At the same time, they can also have unintended negative consequences.

Broad-based price caps and blanket subsidies may benefit not only lower-income households but also affluent ones, resulting in inefficiencies.

Along those lines, the availability of RON95 fuel that is priced significantly below market levels in Malaysia may lead to cross-border leakages, particularly along the Malaysia-Thailand border, according to Gan.

Price controls can also encourage overconsumption. If set below market levels, they may compress margins for producers and retailers, weaken supply incentives and lead to shortages or lower-quality goods.

In Malaysia, cheap sugar has even created tension with public health objectives and burdened the heavily subsidised healthcare system, the S&P analysts remark.

Above all, subsidies come with high public expenditure and, in many cases, become extended drains on state coffers.

NTU’s Dr Chua notes: “(Malaysia’s) fuel subsidy bill is projected to approach RM40 billion in 2026, more than double the amount originally budgeted.”

Lee suggests that the Indonesian government “has had to reprioritise and cut expenditure elsewhere” as a result of commitments not to increase certain fuel prices until the year-end, despite the steep rise in subsidy-related spending.

And although Thailand’s Oil Fuel Fund “looks helpful”, prolonged and pronounced increases in oil prices could mean that the fund’s deficit can widen rapidly, Paracuelles says. That deficit now stands at over 100 billion baht (US$2.98 billion).

If this continues to climb towards 120 billion baht, the government may be pushed to turn to measures such as raising more debt.

“You’re kind of hitting close to that limit already, so I think the response is… try and allow diesel prices to adjust a little bit higher, so (as to) reduce the pressure on the fund,” he says.

Running on fumes

Given that price shocks may be protracted, state-funded price freezes may not be viable in the long term.

Byunghoon Nam, deputy group head and senior economist at Amro, notes that fiscal revenues have generally held up well, on the back of solid economic growth and – ironically – elevated inflation.

“However, borrowing costs are rising, as reflected in higher sovereign bond yields,” he says.

Larger, more persistent energy and food price pressures could increase the strain on public finances and crowd out other spending priorities.

He adds: “Any additional borrowing at elevated interest rates would also raise debt-servicing costs, further limiting fiscal flexibility.”

Says OCBC chief economist Selena Ling: “It’s not just a function of borrowing costs, but also their fiscal position and foreign exchange reserves to sustain those subsidies when global energy or food prices are rising without destabilising their currency, balance of payments or public finances.”

Governments that run fiscal deficits and subsidise prices for certain goods may need to cut back on subsidies or raise new sources of revenue, such as through taxation, she says.

Regional inflation is expected to stay high into early 2027.

“There may be a time lag effect on food prices, even if energy prices stabilise... The risk is for a longer period of elevated and volatile food prices,” says Ling.

The capacity to absorb these prolonged shocks varies by economy. Countries most at risk have large budget deficits, high public debt and sizeable recurring subsidies, as well as current account deficits, reliance on imports, and weak growth, among other factors.

Ling flags economic vulnerability in the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and India, while Singapore, China, Japan, South Korea and Brunei may be more resilient.

Meanwhile, Malaysia’s state-owned energy company Petronas has recorded “some windfall revenues” on climbing oil prices, which Paracuelles says creates “somewhat of an offset”, as these funds can be tapped by the government to defray subsidy costs.

To keep fiscal outlay sustainable, analysts suggest governments implement targeted and temporary support measures – such as handouts or vouchers as direct offsets, which can be more efficient and more equitable than blanket subsidies – while allowing prices to reflect underlying supply and demand conditions.

Price caps and price-related subsidies can be justified as temporary measures, says Nam, particularly when economic and social stability are at risk. “They can buy time to introduce more targeted support.”

But these should be withdrawn as underlying shocks subside, to reduce the fiscal cost and market distortion, he adds.

In the longer run, improving agricultural productivity, diversifying imports and strengthening supply chains provide more sustainable protection against future shocks, Dr Chua adds.

Sticker shock

Even if price shocks are persistent, subsidies and price caps should be phased out gradually, unless there is a very significant threat to macro-financial stability, Nam tells The Business Times.

He adds that sunsetting subsidies should take place with clear communication from the government to the public, to restore market price signals and contain fiscal costs, while targeted support has to be strengthened for the neediest citizens.

Says Paracuelles: “The way to do it is to have a bit of a medium-term transition plan… obviously you can’t worsen the shock by taking out the subsidies in this period. But at the same time, you also don’t want the subsidies to stay there forever.”

But this may be easier said than done.

“In reality, there are societal pressures and political aims involved as well,” Lee acknowledges. Given ground conditions, “policymakers may not necessarily pursue the most economically efficient way” to temper the impact of inflation.

Letting the cost of living go up is generally unpopular with voters.

Continued fuel subsidies are “partly for political considerations”, Paracuelles says, pointing to upcoming elections in Malaysia, as well as to recent protests by Indonesian students in end-October over issues that included rising prices and dwindling subsidies.

Once price controls are introduced, they can be difficult to unwind, with Gan noting that households and businesses “become accustomed to the support” and Ling pointing to an “entitlement mindset”.

“For domestic sociopolitical (reasons), many governments would still want to be seen as proactively shielding their voters from any sharp inflation shock, especially if it hits essentials like food,” Ling says.

“When you increasingly look around the world and see social protests about cost of living and jobs, policymakers would be under pressure to intervene... maybe the ‘here and now’ matters more for governments facing imminent elections.”

data.description:
[SINGAPORE] At supermarket counters from Kuala Lumpur to Manila, global macroeconomic shocks have been jacking up grocery bills – while extracting much higher costs from many governments.

In much of South-east Asia, food carries a significant weight in the consumer price index basket. The prolonged shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up global oil prices, in turn raising transportation, logistics and production costs. Higher fertiliser prices have also made agricultural production costlier, while El Nino-related weather conditions have hit crop yields.

But these cost increases have not uniformly translated to higher consumer prices at the till – partly because some governments have stepped in to cap prices or offer subsidies.

Can they afford to keep intervening to protect household purchasing power?

Established caps

“Countries with larger buffers, stronger currencies or diversified import sources can absorb more of the shock,” says Maybank analyst Brian Lee. “Countries with thin inventories or greater import dependence are considerably more exposed.”

Food prices in the Philippines rose by 6.4 per cent year on year in October, down slightly from inflation of 6.8 per cent in September. Yet rice prices in the country – which produces more than 70 per cent of its rice supply domestically – still picked up at a faster clip.

Food has been a key driver of headline inflation in the Philippines. Catharine Kho, a senior economist at the Asean+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (Amro), notes that heavy rains and flooding disrupted production and deliveries recently, while “higher fuel costs and a weaker peso added to these pressures”.

That’s even though countries such as the Philippines and Indonesia have stockpiles of staples such as rice to serve as what Amro economist Ravisara Hataiseree calls “strategic food reserves… to buffer against sudden supply disruptions”.

At the same time, another factor determining the extent of cost pass-through in developing economies has been state controls on the prices of staples.

Price controls are well established in the region, where policymakers favour mandatory price ceilings for providing immediate and highly visible relief to keep essential goods affordable, while subsidies are preferred for preserving the incentive to produce or supply goods.

As Lee points out: “For staples such as rice, sugar and cooking oil, governments are more inclined to intervene because consumption is widespread, these goods carry high social and political salience, and poorer households spend a larger share of their income on them.”

RHB group chief economist Barnabas Gan comments that food inflation in Malaysia has “remained relatively contained compared to what would otherwise have been expected”, thanks in part to its price controls on a range of grocery staples.

Notably, Malaysia has capped the price of standard coarse white sugar at RM2.85 (US$0.70) per kilogram since 2018. This is among the lowest prices in the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economists Ahmad Mobeen, Lei Yi and Harumi Taguchi, who highlight Malaysia’s “longstanding system of administered prices”.

While direct consumer subsidies for sugar were abolished in 2013, Malaysia has offered incentives to sugar refiners since late 2023, to maintain retail price stability.

Established schemes to tackle fuel costs – another common target of government price controls – have taken on increased prominence in the wake of the global energy shock too.

For instance, Thailand has an oil fuel fund that the government taps to compensate for the increase in retail fuel prices when oil prices surge.

Malaysia uses subsidies to maintain RON95 fuel prices at RM1.99 per litre for eligible residents, while Indonesia keeps subsidised prices for RON90 petrol at 10,000 rupiah per litre and for biodiesel blend at 6,800 rupiah per litre.

He pointed out that Malaysia and Indonesia have seen zero increase in subsidised retail fuel prices since the global energy crisis began with the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East in February. 

At the opposite extreme, the Philippines has no measures to tackle fuel price changes – “so the pass-through is quick and very large”, he said, with 50 to 60 per cent jumps in retail fuel prices in the same period.

Such moves come as more than 80 per cent of Asia-Pacific economies have introduced measures to dampen the pass-through of higher energy prices since February, according to an October regional assessment by the International Monetary Fund.

Conversely, Singapore manages inflation through an exchange rate-based monetary policy and direct household support in the form of vouchers, rebates and payouts. The government explicitly avoids enforcing price ceilings or subsidies to prevent market distortions.

But the National Trades Union Congress-affiliated FairPrice Group (FPG) implements voluntary, time-limited price freezes and discounts on daily essentials. In October, it lowered prices for chicken and eggs – two popular protein staples – until the end of 2026.

In all, FPG has committed more than S$7.5 million worth of savings on groceries and household essentials in 2026, which the retailer attributed in part to concerns over global uncertainty and potential pressure on food and commodity prices.

FPG may be able to negotiate with suppliers for lower prices or absorb some of the higher costs by accepting lower margins, according to Chua Yeow Hwee, an assistant professor of economics at Nanyang Technological University.

S&P’s team adds that the market leader’s pricing decisions may also exert some competitive pressure on other retailers and keep a lid on price increases in the market.

As a profit-seeking entity, FPG is limited by its own financial resources, despite its social mandate, UOB head of research Suan Teck Kin observes.
